OpenClaw Exec Approval Bypass Guide: 4 Approvals to Turn Off Approvals

Apr 2, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Exec Approval Bypass Guide: 4 Approvals to Turn Off Approvals

Section titled “OpenClaw Exec Approval Bypass Guide: 4 Approvals to Turn Off Approvals”

Every cat triggers an approval popup? From principles to config in one guide, plus a real Bootstrap Paradox story.

The Problem: Every Command Needs a Click

Section titled “The Problem: Every Command Needs a Click”

After upgrading to OpenClaw v2026.4.1, you may notice — every shell command the agent runs triggers “Exec approval needed”, requiring manual approval.

Reading a file? Popup. Running grep? Popup. Cat a config? Popup.

It’s not a bug, it’s a feature. OpenClaw’s Exec Approval mechanism is a safety guardrail preventing AI agents from running dangerous commands without your knowledge. Good intention, but for self-managed local instances, the interaction cost is too high.

How It Works: Three Layers Decide a Command’s Fate

Section titled “How It Works: Three Layers Decide a Command’s Fate”

Configured in ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json:

1. Security Level

Section titled “1. Security Level”
ValueBehavior
denyBlock everything
allowlistOnly allowlisted commands pass
fullAllow everything

2. Ask (Popup Behavior)

Section titled “2. Ask (Popup Behavior)”
ValueBehavior
alwaysAsk for every command
on-missAsk only when not allowlisted
offNever ask

3. Ask Fallback (When No UI Available)

Section titled “3. Ask Fallback (When No UI Available)”
ValueBehavior
denyReject
allowlistAllow if allowlisted
fullAllow everything

Default is roughly security: "deny" + ask: "on-miss" — nearly every command triggers a popup.

Three Approaches

Section titled “Three Approaches”

Option 1: Progressive Allowlist (For the Cautious)

Section titled “Option 1: Progressive Allowlist (For the Cautious)”

Choose “Always allow” instead of “Allow once” each time. After a few days, common commands pass silently.

autoAllowSkills: true auto-allows CLI tools referenced by installed skills.

Good for: Shared instances, production, audit-required environments.

Option 2: Full Bypass (For Self-Managed)

Section titled “Option 2: Full Bypass (For Self-Managed)”

Three words: never ask again.

Good for: Local dev machines, personal instances, you-are-the-admin scenarios.

Option 3: Visual Configuration via Control UI

Section titled “Option 3: Visual Configuration via Control UI”

Web UI → Nodes → Exec approvals card. Click to configure, no JSON editing needed.

How To

Section titled “How To”

Config file: ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json

For Option 2, change the "defaults" field to:

Takes effect immediately — no gateway restart needed.

Rolling Back

Section titled “Rolling Back”

Your allowlist is preserved.

Per-Agent Fine Control

Section titled “Per-Agent Fine Control”

For multi-agent setups, only unlock specific agents:

defaults covers agents without individual config. agents.<id> overrides defaults.

Appendix: The Bootstrap Paradox

Section titled “Appendix: The Bootstrap Paradox”

Here’s the actual process of turning off Exec Approval — note the recursive irony:

Approval #1: Search for exec-approvals docs

Approval #2: Read the official documentation

Approval #3: View current config

Approval #4: Modify config to disable approvals

“Last approval ever 🎉 After this one, exec approval will never bother you again.”

4 approvals to complete “turn off approvals.” Classic Bootstrap Paradox — you need the key to get the key. At least you only need to forge it once.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
Who You AreRecommendedKey Config
Local dev / PersonalFull bypasssecurity: full + ask: off
Shared / ProductionProgressive allowlistsecurity: allowlist + ask: on-miss + autoAllowSkills
Maximum securityManual allowlistsecurity: allowlist + ask: always

Exec Approval is good design, but good design must match the use case. For self-managing admins, popups aren’t security — they’re friction.

Based on OpenClaw v2026.4.1, config file ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json.

OpenClaw Local Upgrade Log: 2026.3.28 → 2026.4.1 (with npm Install Interruption Fix)

Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Local Upgrade Log: 2026.3.28 → 2026.4.1

Section titled “OpenClaw Local Upgrade Log: 2026.3.28 → 2026.4.1”

Date: 2026-04-02 | Platform: macOS (arm64) | Node: v24.9.0

Background

Section titled “Background”

Local OpenClaw at 2026.3.28, npm registry has 2026.4.1. Routine version upgrade.

Upgrade Steps

Section titled “Upgrade Steps”

1. Check Version Gap

Section titled “1. Check Version Gap”

2. First Attempt — SIGKILL

Section titled “2. First Attempt — SIGKILL”

Process killed by system SIGKILL — likely memory pressure or install timeout. macOS kills memory-heavy processes under pressure.

3. Second Attempt — ENOTEMPTY

Section titled “3. Second Attempt — ENOTEMPTY”

Error:

Cause: The SIGKILL-interrupted install left behind a .openclaw-* temporary directory. npm can’t complete the rename.

4. Clean Up + Reinstall ✅

Section titled “4. Clean Up + Reinstall ✅”

Output:

5. Verify + Restart Gateway

Section titled “5. Verify + Restart Gateway”

Gotchas

Section titled “Gotchas”
IssueCauseFix
SIGKILL during installSystem memory pressure or timeoutRetry
ENOTEMPTY errorLeftover .openclaw-* temp directoryrm -rf node_modules/.openclaw-* then reinstall

General Tips

Section titled “General Tips”
  • After interrupted npm global installs, check for .package-name-* temp directories under node_modules/ and clean before retrying
  • Always openclaw gateway restart after upgrading — otherwise the gateway runs old code
  • Gateway restart resets exec approval policies — re-approval required

Version Summary

Section titled “Version Summary”
ItemBeforeAfter
OpenClaw2026.3.282026.4.1
Node.jsv24.9.0v24.9.0 (unchanged)
Package changes—+49 / -706 / ~482
Install time—31 seconds

Upgrade Checklist

Section titled “Upgrade Checklist”
  • npm view openclaw version — check latest
  • npm install -g openclaw@<version>
  • If ENOTEMPTY → clean .openclaw-* temp dirs, retry
  • openclaw --version — verify
  • openclaw gateway restart
  • Verify gateway is running

Applicable to any npm-global-installed OpenClaw instance.

OpenClaw Remote Upgrade Guide: Upgrading a Mac Mini Node via Tailscale + SSH

Apr 2, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Remote Upgrade Guide: Upgrading a Mac Mini Node via Tailscale + SSH

Section titled “OpenClaw Remote Upgrade Guide: Upgrading a Mac Mini Node via Tailscale + SSH”

Date: 2026-04-02 Target: Mac Mini M1 node (macOS 26.3.1) Method: Tailscale + SSH tunnel Upgrade path: OpenClaw 2026.3.28 → 2026.4.1

Background

Section titled “Background”

We have a Mac Mini M1 running as an OpenClaw node, connected via Tailscale mesh networking. The admin manages it through a local SSH tunnel (localhost:<local-port> → <tailscale-ip>:<remote-port>).

Pre-upgrade state:

  • OS: macOS 26.3.1 (arm64)
  • Node.js: v25.8.2 (Homebrew, at /opt/homebrew/bin)
  • OpenClaw: 2026.3.28
  • Gateway service: LaunchDaemon (system-level plist)

Gotchas

Section titled “Gotchas”

Gotcha 1: Non-Interactive SSH Can’t Find Commands

Section titled “Gotcha 1: Non-Interactive SSH Can’t Find Commands”

Why: Non-interactive SSH doesn’t load .zshrc / .zprofile, so Homebrew-installed Node/npm isn’t in PATH.

Fix: Manually export PATH:

Gotcha 2: npm Install Timeout Kills SSH Session

Section titled “Gotcha 2: npm Install Timeout Kills SSH Session”

Running npm install -g openclaw@latest directly over SSH — the large package download gets killed by the local exec timeout mechanism (SIGKILL).

Attempted workarounds:

  • ServerAliveInterval=30 → Didn’t help (it’s a local exec timeout, not SSH keepalive)
  • nohup ... & → Log file was 0 bytes (zsh non-interactive nohup redirection is unreliable)

Gotcha 3: No Internet Connectivity

Section titled “Gotcha 3: No Internet Connectivity”

Mid-upgrade, discovered the node had no internet access:

  • registry.npmjs.org → curl timeout
  • registry.npmmirror.com → DNS failure (ENOTFOUND)
  • brew install tmux → Same timeout

Lesson: Always test connectivity before attempting upgrades.

Gotcha 4: nohup + zsh Non-Interactive Is Unreliable

Section titled “Gotcha 4: nohup + zsh Non-Interactive Is Unreliable”

zsh in non-interactive mode has inconsistent stdout/stderr redirection with nohup. Use tmux instead.

Gotcha 5: LaunchDaemon Requires sudo

Section titled “Gotcha 5: LaunchDaemon Requires sudo”

The gateway runs as a LaunchDaemon (system-level service), so restarts require sudo:

For non-interactive SSH, sudo needs password via stdin (production environments should use sudoers NOPASSWD or a secrets manager):

The Working Procedure

Section titled “The Working Procedure”

After network recovery, the complete upgrade steps:

1. Test Network Connectivity

Section titled “1. Test Network Connectivity”

2. Run Upgrade Inside tmux (Survives SSH Disconnects)

Section titled “2. Run Upgrade Inside tmux (Survives SSH Disconnects)”

3. Check Progress Periodically

Section titled “3. Check Progress Periodically”

Output:

4. Verify Version

Section titled “4. Verify Version”

5. Restart Gateway (LaunchDaemon)

Section titled “5. Restart Gateway (LaunchDaemon)”

6. Verify Gateway Is Running

Section titled “6. Verify Gateway Is Running”

Lessons Learned

Section titled “Lessons Learned”
IssueLesson
Non-interactive SSH has no PATHAlways manually export PATH for remote commands
Long npm installs get killedUse tmux — never run long commands over bare SSH
nohup logs emptyzsh non-interactive + nohup redirection is unreliable; tmux is more robust
No internetTest connectivity before upgrading — don’t wait for npm to hang
LaunchDaemon needs sudoThe cost of headless Mac with LaunchDaemon — remote restart requires sudo access
Plaintext passwordsUse sudoers NOPASSWD or a secrets manager in production

Before/After

Section titled “Before/After”
ItemBeforeAfter
OpenClaw2026.3.282026.4.1
Node.jsv25.8.2v25.8.2 (unchanged)
Upgrade time—~1 minute (once network was up)

Remote Upgrade Checklist

Section titled “Remote Upgrade Checklist”

For future remote OpenClaw node upgrades:

  • Test internet connectivity (curl registry.npmjs.org)
  • Confirm tmux is installed
  • Run npm install -g openclaw@latest inside tmux
  • Verify version with openclaw --version
  • Restart gateway (launchctl bootout + bootstrap)
  • Verify HTTP probe returns 200
  • Clean up tmux session

Based on a real remote upgrade session. Applicable to any Mac Mini OpenClaw node managed via Tailscale/SSH.

Updating a Weekly Report by Chatting with OpenClaw: A Real Example of AI OpenClaw Operating Excel

Apr 2, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Updating a Weekly Report by Chatting with OpenClaw: A Real Example of AI OpenClaw Operating Excel

Section titled “Updating a Weekly Report by Chatting with OpenClaw: A Real Example of AI OpenClaw Operating Excel”

Date: 2026-04-02 Tools: OpenClaw + Python openpyxl

Background

Section titled “Background”

Every week, I need to update an Excel weekly report. The process is fixed, but tedious:

  1. Copy last week’s file and update the date in the filename
  2. Move completed items from the “Recent Releases” sheet to the “Release History” sheet
  3. Add new feedback to the “Recent Plans” sheet
  4. Record this week’s release in the “Recent Releases” sheet
  5. Fix formatting issues such as text wrapping

This time, I did not open Excel at all. Instead, I used OpenClaw WebChat and let AI OpenClaw complete the entire workflow automatically.

Process

Section titled “Process”

1. Copy the weekly report and update the filename

Section titled “1. Copy the weekly report and update the filename”

I told OpenClaw to copy last week’s report and change the date in the filename from last week to this week.

OpenClaw automatically generated a Python script to copy and rename the file.

2. Archive completed items

Section titled “2. Archive completed items”

I told OpenClaw to move the four completed items from the “Recent Releases” sheet to the top of the “Release History” sheet, and then clear the data area in “Recent Releases.”

The moved items included:

  • Keep two decimal places
  • Fix multiple issue feedback items
  • Device log analysis

OpenClaw read the sheet data, inserted the rows into the target sheet, and cleaned the source data in one go.

3. Add new feedback to recent plans

Section titled “3. Add new feedback to recent plans”

I described two new issue feedback items in chat, and OpenClaw wrote them into the corresponding sheet:

TypeSummary
Issue feedbackUsers cannot see device details → optimize the design solution
Issue feedbackCountdown is not displayed → layout adjustment + message reminder

4. Add this week’s release record to recent releases

Section titled “4. Add this week’s release record to recent releases”

I described this week’s release content, and OpenClaw wrote it into the “Recent Releases” sheet:

Waiting time adjustment, calculator entry

Note: OpenClaw initially placed it in the release history sheet by mistake. After I pointed it out in chat, it immediately corrected it to the right place.

5. Fix formatting

Section titled “5. Fix formatting”

I asked OpenClaw to check all non-empty cells and ensure the Wrap Text property was set correctly.

Technical implementation

Section titled “Technical implementation”
ItemDescription
OpenClawOpenClaw
Excel libraryPython openpyxl
Interaction methodWebChat natural language conversation
WorkflowUser describes the task → OpenClaw generates a Python script → execute → feedback → user confirms/corrects → iterate

Why use AI OpenClaw to operate Excel?

Section titled “Why use AI OpenClaw to operate Excel?”

Good use cases

Section titled “Good use cases”
  • Repeated weekly reports: the structure is the same every week, only the content changes
  • Multi-sheet coordination: moving data across sheets is easy to get wrong manually
  • Consistent formatting: checking Wrap Text cell by cell is tedious
  • Remote operation: you can finish the task by chatting on your phone even when away from your computer

Less suitable scenarios

Section titled “Less suitable scenarios”
  • Complex formulas and chart operations
  • Tasks that require visual confirmation of layout
  • One-off tasks where manual work is faster

Key advantages

Section titled “Key advantages”

Correctable iteration: if OpenClaw makes a mistake, such as writing to the wrong sheet, I can correct it through chat. This is more intuitive than debugging a script manually.

Zero learning curve: there is no need to learn the openpyxl API or write code. I can simply describe the action in natural language, like “move these rows over there.”

Takeaways

Section titled “Takeaways”
  1. Be specific: do not say “update the weekly report”; say “move the four items from Recent Releases to the top of Release History”
  2. Work step by step: let OpenClaw do one thing at a time, then confirm before continuing
  3. Check promptly: after each step, ask OpenClaw to read back the result for verification
  4. Allow mistakes: OpenClaw may put something in the wrong place, but the cost of correction is very low—just say it

The entire process was completed without opening the Excel application. Through OpenClaw chat, I finished copying, archiving, adding updates, and fixing formatting in the weekly report.

Tags:
  • OpenClaw
  • Excel
  • AI Automation
  • Weekly Report

Claude Code 2.1.89 Changelog Deep Analysis

Apr 1, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Release date: Late 2025 – Early 2026 (estimated) Analysis date: 2026-04-01

This article dissects every change in Claude Code 2.1.89, analyzing the problem context, use cases with examples, and caveats, while drawing lateral comparisons with Codex CLI and Gemini CLI, and closing with a look at evolution trends.

Table of Contents

Section titled “Table of Contents”
  1. New Features (Added)
  2. Bug Fixes (Fixed)
  3. UX Improvements (Improved)
  4. Behavioral Changes (Changed)
  5. Miscellaneous & Easter Eggs
  6. Summary & Trends

1. New Features

Section titled “1. New Features”

1.1 "defer" Decision for PreToolUse Hooks

Section titled “1.1 "defer" Decision for PreToolUse Hooks”

What changed: The PreToolUse hook can now return "defer" as a permission decision. Headless sessions (-p mode) pause at that tool call, and the user later resumes with -p --resume, at which point the hook is re-evaluated.

Problem context: In CI/CD or automation pipelines, Claude Code runs in headless mode (-p). Previously, hooks could only return allow or deny. When human approval was needed (e.g., executing a dangerous command or writing to production config), you had to either allow everything or deny everything—no middle ground.

Use cases & examples:

In a CI pipeline, Claude Code encounters rm -rf build/ and pauses. After an ops engineer reviews the action:

The hook re-evaluates (it can now check an external approval system’s status) and decides to allow or deny.

Caveats:

  • --resume would hang if the deferred tool input exceeded 64KB or lacked a deferred marker (this release also fixes that issue).
  • You need to design a proper polling/callback mechanism for external approval state.

Cross-tool comparison:

DimensionClaude CodeCodex CLIGemini CLI
Hook systemPreToolUse/PostToolUse with allow/deny/deferNo hook system; relies on global --approval-mode switchNo hook system
Pause/Resumedefer + --resumeNot supportedNot supported
CI integrationFirst-class citizenBasic supportLimited

Trend: This signals Claude Code’s evolution toward a “composable AI Agent runtime”—not just a CLI tool, but an execution engine that can be embedded in enterprise approval workflows. We may eventually see webhook-callback-style defer (no manual resume needed).

1.2 CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1 Flicker-Free Rendering

Section titled “1.2 CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1 Flicker-Free Rendering”

What changed: A new environment variable enables alt-screen-based flicker-free rendering with virtualized scroll-back.

Problem context: Claude Code’s TUI (terminal UI) tends to flicker and jitter during long streaming output, especially under iTerm2/tmux. This happens because the default main-screen rendering mode causes each redraw to affect the scroll buffer.

Use cases:

Ideal for:

  • Users running Claude Code inside tmux
  • Users on low-refresh-rate terminal emulators
  • Extended sessions (coding marathons)

Caveats:

  • In alt-screen mode, session content is not preserved in the terminal scroll buffer after exit (similar to how vim restores the screen on quit).
  • Marked as “opt-in,” indicating it’s not mature enough to be the default and may have edge-case compatibility issues.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Ink (React for CLI) rendering with built-in alt-screen; less flickering but lower customizability.
  • Gemini CLI: Python-based Rich/Textual rendering; moderate flicker control.

Trend: Terminal AI tools are moving from “functional” to “polished.” Rendering quality is becoming a core UX differentiator. Alt-screen with full virtual scrolling may become the default in the future.

1.3 PermissionDenied Hook

Section titled “1.3 PermissionDenied Hook”

What changed: A new PermissionDenied hook fires after the auto-mode classifier rejects an operation. Returning {retry: true} lets the model retry.

Problem context: In auto mode, Claude Code has a safety classifier that automatically rejects operations deemed dangerous. But sometimes these are false positives, especially when command semantics are complex. Previously, users could only manually retry or switch to manual mode.

Use cases: A custom hook script checks whether the rejected command is on a whitelist:

For example, docker compose down might be misclassified as a dangerous delete command—the hook can automatically allow a retry.

Caveats:

  • retry: true just tells the model it can retry; it doesn’t bypass permissions—the model may take a different approach.
  • Overusing this hook undermines the safety classifier’s protective value.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Has three modes (suggest / auto-edit / full-auto), no fine-grained hooks.
  • Gemini CLI: Uses Google’s safety filters with no user-customizable recovery mechanism.

1.4 Named Subagents in @ Mentions

Section titled “1.4 Named Subagents in @ Mentions”

What changed: Named subagents now appear in @-mention autocomplete suggestions.

Problem context: Claude Code supports background subagents for task execution. Previously, users could only manage subagents through /agents or the API—referencing them in conversation was inconvenient.

Use cases: While coding, you’ve launched a background subagent for testing:

The @ autocomplete dropdown now shows named subagents for direct reference.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: No subagent support.
  • Gemini CLI: No subagent support.

Trend: Multi-agent orchestration is evolving from a “background concept” to a “first-class interactive object.” In the future, @ may unify references to files, tools, agents, and MCP resources.

1.5 Non-Blocking MCP Connections

Section titled “1.5 Non-Blocking MCP Connections”

What changed: MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true completely skips MCP connection waiting in -p mode; additionally, --mcp-config server connections are capped at 5 seconds.

Problem context: MCP (Model Context Protocol) server connections can be slow (network latency, slow server startup). In CI scenarios where only partial MCP capabilities are needed, waiting for all servers to connect significantly delays startup.

Use cases:

Caveats:

  • In non-blocking mode, if the model calls an MCP tool that hasn’t connected yet, it will fail.
  • The 5-second timeout may be too short for cold-starting SSE servers.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: No MCP support.
  • Gemini CLI: Supports MCP but has no non-blocking option; failed connections are simply skipped.

Trend: MCP connection management is moving toward a “progressive readiness” model—start first, connect tools on demand, rather than requiring everything to be ready at launch.

1.6 Notifications & Retry for Auto Mode Rejections

Section titled “1.6 Notifications & Retry for Auto Mode Rejections”

What changed: Commands rejected in auto mode now display a notification and appear in /permissions → Recent tab, where you can press r to retry.

Problem context: Previously, auto mode silently swallowed rejections—users might not know why a task didn’t complete.

Use cases: Claude Code in auto mode attempts git push --force and gets rejected. A notification pops up in the terminal: “Permission denied: git push —force.” The user opens /permissions → Recent, sees the record, and presses r to allow and retry.

Caveats:

  • This balances security with usability—keeping users informed without interrupting their workflow.

2. Bug Fixes

Section titled “2. Bug Fixes”

2.1 Permission Rules for Symlinked Paths

Section titled “2.1 Permission Rules for Symlinked Paths”

What changed: Edit(//path/**) and Read(//path/**) rules now check the resolved symlink target path rather than the requested path.

Problem context: Security vulnerability: an attacker could create a symlink /safe/link → /etc/passwd. If permission rules only checked /safe/**, protected files could be read/written through the symlink.

Use cases:

Caveats:

  • If your project has legitimate symlinks pointing to external directories, you’ll need to add explicit allow rules.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses sandboxing (Docker/seatbelt) to restrict file access at the OS level, not relying on path rules.
  • Gemini CLI: Simpler permission model with no fine-grained path rules.

2.2 Voice Mode Fixes (Multiple)

Section titled “2.2 Voice Mode Fixes (Multiple)”

What changed:

  1. Fixed push-to-talk not activating with certain modifier key combinations
  2. Fixed voice mode reporting “WebSocket upgrade rejected with HTTP 101” on Windows
  3. Fixed voice mode failing to request microphone permissions on macOS Apple Silicon

Problem context: Voice mode is a differentiating feature for Claude Code, but cross-platform compatibility has been a persistent pain point: Windows handles WebSocket differently, macOS Apple Silicon has a unique permissions model, and different terminal emulators handle key bindings differently.

Caveats:

  • Voice mode is still experimental and may not work in SSH/remote sessions.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: No voice mode.
  • Gemini CLI: No voice mode.

2.3 Windows CRLF and Markdown Hard Break Fixes

Section titled “2.3 Windows CRLF and Markdown Hard Break Fixes”

What changed: Edit/Write tools no longer double up CRLF on Windows (causing double blank lines) and no longer strip Markdown hard breaks (trailing double spaces).

Problem context: Windows uses \r\n as line endings. If the tool converts \n to \r\n but the input is already \r\n, it becomes \r\r\n, producing double blank lines. Meanwhile, trailing double spaces in Markdown (which represent <br>) were being incorrectly trimmed.

Use cases: Editing .md files on Windows: before the fix, blank lines doubled on every save; Markdown table alignment and other scenarios requiring trailing spaces were broken.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Also uses patch-based editing, but runs in a Docker sandbox (Linux), sidestepping CRLF issues.
  • Gemini CLI: Uses Python’s file handling under the hood, which handles line endings more maturely.

2.4 StructuredOutput Schema Caching Bug

Section titled “2.4 StructuredOutput Schema Caching Bug”

What changed: Fixed a StructuredOutput schema cache bug that caused ~50% failure rate when using multiple schemas.

Problem context: The --json-schema feature lets Claude Code produce structured output. When different schemas were used within the same session, a flawed cache key caused the wrong schema to be returned, failing JSON validation.

Use cases:

Caveats:

  • A 50% failure rate means any automation pipeline relying on multiple schemas was unreliable before this fix.

2.5 Memory Leak in Long Sessions

Section titled “2.5 Memory Leak in Long Sessions”

What changed: Fixed a memory leak caused by large JSON inputs being retained as LRU cache keys.

Problem context: The LRU cache used the full JSON string of input content as its key. When inputs were large (e.g., reading large file contents), these strings stayed in memory and were never garbage collected. In extended sessions (e.g., 8-hour coding marathons), the Node.js process memory would climb continuously.

Use cases: After several hours of continuous Claude Code use and reading multiple large files, process memory grows from 300MB to 2GB+, and the terminal starts lagging.

Caveats:

  • For long sessions, periodically using /clear or /compact is recommended.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses React/Ink rendering; also exhibits memory growth but manifests differently.
  • Gemini CLI: Python runtime with a different GC strategy; long sessions may have similar issues.

2.6 Crash When Deleting Messages from >50MB Session Files

Section titled “2.6 Crash When Deleting Messages from >50MB Session Files”

What changed: Fixed a crash when deleting messages from session files exceeding 50MB.

Problem context: Session transcript files grow with conversation length. Sessions that heavily use tools (especially reading large files) can easily exceed 50MB. The full-file parse-and-rewrite operation when deleting messages caused out-of-memory errors or timeout crashes on oversized files.

2.7 LSP Server Zombie State Fix

Section titled “2.7 LSP Server Zombie State Fix”

What changed: After an LSP server crash, it no longer enters a zombie state; instead, it automatically restarts on the next request.

Problem context: Claude Code integrates LSP (Language Server Protocol) for code intelligence (go-to-definition, type checking, etc.). When an LSP server crashed, it previously entered an unusable state, silently failing all subsequent LSP operations until the user manually restarted the session.

Use cases: In a TypeScript project, editing a massive .d.ts file causes tsserver to OOM and crash. Before the fix, you had to exit and reenter Claude Code; after the fix, the next LSP call auto-recovers.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: No LSP integration.
  • Gemini CLI: No LSP integration.
  • VS Code/Cursor: Auto-restarting LSP is standard.

Trend: Claude Code is approaching IDE-level robustness.

2.8 CJK/Emoji Prompt History Loss

Section titled “2.8 CJK/Emoji Prompt History Loss”

What changed: Fixed prompt history entries containing CJK or emoji being silently discarded at 4KB boundaries in ~/.claude/history.jsonl.

Problem context: The JSONL file is read in 4KB chunks. CJK characters and emoji use multi-byte UTF-8 encoding (3–4 bytes). When a character straddles a 4KB boundary, it gets truncated, causing JSON parse failure and the entire record being silently dropped.

Use cases: Chinese/Japanese/Korean users frequently using Claude Code would find their prompt history missing (pressing the up arrow couldn’t find previous commands).

Caveats:

  • This bug affected a large number of Asian users; the fix is significant.
  • Similar UTF-8 boundary bugs exist in many tools.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Node.js readline; CJK handling is delegated to system libraries.
  • Gemini CLI: Python’s Unicode handling is relatively mature, though similar boundary issues may still occur.

2.9 Inaccurate /stats Token Counts

Section titled “2.9 Inaccurate /stats Token Counts”

What changed: Fixed /stats not counting subagent token usage, and fixed loss of 30+ day historical data when the statistics cache format changed.

Problem context: Users rely on /stats to monitor API usage and costs. Missing subagent usage means significantly underestimating actual consumption, especially for heavy background agent users.

2.10 --resume and --continue Recovery Issues

Section titled “2.10 --resume and --continue Recovery Issues”

What changed: Fixed -p --resume hanging when deferred tool input exceeds 64KB or lacks a deferred marker, and fixed --continue not restoring deferred tools.

Problem context: Companion fix for the defer feature in §1.1—multiple edge cases existed in the resume path when defer was first introduced.

2.11 macOS Deep Links Fix

Section titled “2.11 macOS Deep Links Fix”

What changed: Fixed claude-cli:// deep links not opening on macOS.

Use cases: Clicking a claude-cli://open?q=... link in a webpage to open Claude Code in the terminal with a pre-filled prompt. Commonly used in documentation, tutorials, and team sharing.

2.12 MCP Error Truncation Fix

Section titled “2.12 MCP Error Truncation Fix”

What changed: MCP tools returning multi-element error content no longer show only the first content block.

Problem context: MCP servers may return complex error information (e.g., error description + stack trace + suggested fix across multiple content blocks). After truncation, users could only see “something went wrong” without the critical diagnostic details.

2.13 System Context Loss When Sending Images via SDK

Section titled “2.13 System Context Loss When Sending Images via SDK”

What changed: Fixed skill reminders and other system context being dropped when sending messages containing images through the SDK.

Problem context: In the SDK’s message serialization, the special handling path for images missed the system context injection step.

2.14 Hook Path Normalization

Section titled “2.14 Hook Path Normalization”

What changed: PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks now provide an absolute file_path for Write/Edit/Read tools.

Problem context: Previously, the path might be relative, requiring hook scripts to resolve it themselves—an error-prone process. The fix aligns behavior with the documentation.

2.15 Autocompact Infinite Loop Fix ⭐

Section titled “2.15 Autocompact Infinite Loop Fix ⭐”

What changed: When context refills immediately after compaction (3 consecutive times), the system now stops and reports an actionable error instead of looping infinitely and burning API calls.

Problem context: This was a severe cost and usability bug. When project configuration caused large amounts of context to be injected (e.g., deeply nested CLAUDE.md files, verbose skill descriptions), compaction would clear them only for them to be re-injected immediately, triggering another compaction—an infinite loop. Each compaction is an API call, potentially consuming enormous amounts of tokens without the user’s knowledge.

Use cases: In a large monorepo with multiple layers of nested CLAUDE.md files, each compaction re-injects all of them, pushing token count right back to the threshold. After dozens of cycles, the user discovers their API usage has skyrocketed.

Caveats:

  • If you encounter this error, check for excessive CLAUDE.md nesting or overly verbose skill descriptions.
  • Understand this fix in conjunction with §2.17 (CLAUDE.md duplicate injection).

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: No auto-compact feature; when context is full, it simply errors out.
  • Gemini CLI: Different context management strategy; no equivalent loop issue.

Trend: Automatic context management is essential for long-session usability, but needs smarter strategies (e.g., incremental compaction, selective retention, importance scoring).

2.16 Prompt Cache Hit Rate Degradation Fix

Section titled “2.16 Prompt Cache Hit Rate Degradation Fix”

What changed: Fixed prompt cache misses in long sessions caused by tool schema byte changes.

Problem context: Anthropic’s API prompt cache relies on prefix matching. If tool schemas change slightly during a session (e.g., an MCP tool dynamically updates its description), the entire prompt prefix is invalidated, causing a cache miss. Every request must then reprocess the full context, dramatically increasing latency and cost.

Caveats:

  • This is a “hidden cost” bug—users might just feel “things got slower” without realizing it’s a cache miss.

2.17 Nested CLAUDE.md Duplicate Injection

Section titled “2.17 Nested CLAUDE.md Duplicate Injection”

What changed: Fixed nested CLAUDE.md files being injected dozens of times during long sessions with multiple file reads.

Problem context: Claude Code automatically discovers and loads CLAUDE.md files at every level of the project. In long sessions, as file operations accumulate, the deduplication logic breaks down, and the same CLAUDE.md might be added to context 20–30 times.

Use cases: A monorepo where each package has its own CLAUDE.md:

During a long session with frequent cross-package operations, all CLAUDE.md files get re-injected with each operation.

2.18 --resume Compatibility Crash

Section titled “2.18 --resume Compatibility Crash”

What changed: Fixed --resume crashing when the transcript contains tool results from older CLI versions or interrupted writes.

Problem context: Rapid CLI iteration means tool result serialization formats change. Resuming old sessions may encounter format incompatibilities.

2.19 Misleading “Rate limit reached” Error

Section titled “2.19 Misleading “Rate limit reached” Error”

What changed: When the API actually returns an entitlement error, the misleading “Rate limit reached” message is replaced with the real error and an actionable prompt.

Problem context: Users seeing “Rate limit reached” assume it’s temporary throttling and wait to retry. But the actual cause might be:

  • Plan doesn’t support the feature
  • API key lacks access to the model
  • Organization quota is exhausted

After the fix, messages like “Your plan does not include access to claude-opus-4. Upgrade at…” are displayed instead.

2.20 Hook if Conditions Not Matching Compound Commands

Section titled “2.20 Hook if Conditions Not Matching Compound Commands”

What changed: Fixed hook if conditions not matching compound commands like ls && git push or commands with environment variable prefixes like FOO=bar git push.

Problem context:

Previously, git push would match, but ls && git push and FOO=bar git push wouldn’t. Attack vector: a model could bypass hooks by chaining commands.

2.21 Devanagari and Other Combining Mark Text Truncation

Section titled “2.21 Devanagari and Other Combining Mark Text Truncation”

What changed: Fixed Hindi and other scripts using combining marks being truncated in assistant output.

Problem context: In complex writing systems like Devanagari, a single visual character may consist of a base character plus multiple combining marks (vowel signs, virama, etc.). Truncating by byte or code point may break in the middle of combining marks, causing garbled text or data loss.

Caveats:

  • Internationalization support is a long-tail need for CLI tools, but it’s a critical issue for specific user populations.

2.22 Windows-Specific Fixes

Section titled “2.22 Windows-Specific Fixes”

This release includes multiple Windows fixes, reflecting increased commitment to Windows platform support:

  1. Shift+Enter submits instead of inserting newline — Key code handling difference in Windows Terminal Preview 1.25
  2. PowerShell stderr false failure reports — Commands like git push write progress to stderr; PowerShell 5.1 treats this as failure
  3. Edit tool OOM on >1GiB files — Large files loaded entirely into memory

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Windows support via WSL/Docker; limited native Windows support.
  • Gemini CLI: Python-based cross-platform; decent native Windows support but weaker terminal interaction.

2.23 Streaming Render Jitter in iTerm2 + tmux

Section titled “2.23 Streaming Render Jitter in iTerm2 + tmux”

What changed: Fixed periodic UI jitter during streaming output when using iTerm2 inside tmux.

Problem context: tmux and terminal emulators communicate via escape sequences. High-frequency refreshes from streaming output conflict with tmux’s pane redraw mechanism, causing visible jitter.

2.24 Other Terminal Rendering Fixes

Section titled “2.24 Other Terminal Rendering Fixes”
  • Collapsed search/read group badges duplicated — UI components duplicated during parallel tool calls
  • Notifications not clearing promptly — invalidates field not working
  • Prompt briefly disappearing after submission — Background message race condition
  • Main-screen rendering artifacts — Residual artifacts after layout shift

3. UX Improvements

Section titled “3. UX Improvements”

3.1 Tool Summary Optimization

Section titled “3.1 Tool Summary Optimization”

What changed: ls/tree/du now display “Listed N directories” instead of “Read N files.”

Problem context: Semantic accuracy—listing directories isn’t “reading files,” and the previous wording was confusing for users.

3.2 Stale-Edit Warning for Bash Tool ⭐

Section titled “3.2 Stale-Edit Warning for Bash Tool ⭐”

What changed: The Bash tool now warns when a formatter/linter command modifies a file that was previously read.

Problem context: Typical scenario:

  1. Claude Code reads app.tsx
  2. Claude Code runs prettier --write app.tsx (formatting modifies the file)
  3. Claude Code generates an edit based on step 1’s content → overwrites prettier’s changes

After the fix, step 2 warns “This command modified a file you previously read,” prompting the model to re-read.

Caveats:

  • This is a clever heuristic—detecting whether a command modified a known file.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses git diff to detect changes but doesn’t proactively warn.
  • Gemini CLI: No equivalent mechanism.

3.3 @ Mention Sorting Optimization

Section titled “3.3 @ Mention Sorting Optimization”

What changed: Source files now rank higher than same-named MCP resources in mention autocomplete.

Problem context: As MCP resources multiply, the completion list can be overwhelmed by MCP resources. In most cases, users want to reference local files.

3.4 PowerShell Version-Specific Guidance

Section titled “3.4 PowerShell Version-Specific Guidance”

What changed: The PowerShell tool now provides different syntax guidance based on version (5.1 vs 7+).

Problem context: PS 5.1 (built into Windows) and PS 7+ (cross-platform) have significant syntax differences (e.g., ??= operator, ForEach-Object -Parallel are only available in 7+).

4. Behavioral Changes

Section titled “4. Behavioral Changes”

4.1 Edit Tool No Longer Requires Prior Read

Section titled “4.1 Edit Tool No Longer Requires Prior Read”

What changed: Files previously viewed via Bash’s sed -n or cat can now be edited directly without first using the Read tool.

Problem context: Previously, the Edit tool required a file to have been read by the Read tool first (for version validation). But if the model had viewed file contents through Bash and then called Edit, it would error out demanding a Read first—wasting a tool call and tokens.

Caveats:

  • Reduces unnecessary tool calls, improving efficiency.

4.2 Oversized Hook Output Stored to Disk

Section titled “4.2 Oversized Hook Output Stored to Disk”

What changed: Hook output exceeding 50K characters is stored to a disk file; only the file path and a preview are injected into context.

Problem context: Malicious or poorly designed hooks may produce massive output. Injecting it directly into context would:

  1. Rapidly fill the context window
  2. Waste tokens
  3. Potentially trigger the autocompact infinite loop

4.3 cleanupPeriodDays: 0 Validation Error

Section titled “4.3 cleanupPeriodDays: 0 Validation Error”

What changed: Setting this to 0 now throws a validation error; previously, it silently disabled transcript persistence.

Problem context: Users might set it to 0 thinking it means “unlimited” (a common off-by-one semantic), when the actual effect is “never retain”—causing all session history to be lost.

4.4 Thinking Summaries No Longer Generated by Default

Section titled “4.4 Thinking Summaries No Longer Generated by Default”

What changed: Interactive sessions no longer generate thinking summaries by default; you can restore them with showThinkingSummaries: true.

Problem context: Thinking summaries display a digest of the model’s reasoning process to the user. They add token consumption and latency, and most users don’t need them—they’re only useful when debugging model reasoning.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Has --reasoning-summary option, off by default.
  • Gemini CLI: Thinking process displayed by default, no summary concept.

4.5 /env Applies to PowerShell

Section titled “4.5 /env Applies to PowerShell”

What changed: Environment variables set via /env now also apply to PowerShell tool commands.

4.6 Simplified /usage Display

Section titled “4.6 Simplified /usage Display”

What changed: Pro and Enterprise plans no longer show the redundant “Current week (Sonnet only)” progress bar.

5. Miscellaneous & Easter Eggs

Section titled “5. Miscellaneous & Easter Eggs”

5.1 Documentation & Behavior Normalization

Section titled “5.1 Documentation & Behavior Normalization”
  • TaskCreated hook event documented along with its blocking behavior
  • Ctrl+B backgrounding preserves task notifications
  • PowerShell 5.1 parameter hardening (arguments containing double quotes + spaces trigger a prompt instead of auto-allow)
  • Pasting !command enters bash mode
  • Image pasting no longer inserts a trailing space

5.2 /buddy April Fools’ Easter Egg 🐣

Section titled “5.2 /buddy April Fools’ Easter Egg 🐣”

What changed: April 1st exclusive—hatch a little creature that watches you code.

Analysis: This reflects engineering culture. Great CLI tools should have soul and humor. /buddy is in the same vein as:

  • VS Code’s Power Mode extension
  • GitHub Copilot Chat’s emoji reactions
  • Vim’s :help holy-grail

6. Summary & Trends

Section titled “6. Summary & Trends”

6.1 Release Profile

Section titled “6.1 Release Profile”

With 60+ changes, this release reveals several clear themes:

ThemeShareRepresentative Changes
Robustness/Stability~40%Memory leak, OOM, infinite loop, zombie process fixes
Windows/Cross-platform~20%CRLF, PowerShell, Shift+Enter
Hooks/Automation~15%defer, PermissionDenied, if condition fixes
Terminal Rendering~15%Flickering, jitter, combining marks, notifications
Internationalization~10%CJK history loss, Devanagari truncation

6.2 Competitive Landscape

Section titled “6.2 Competitive Landscape”

Claude Code leads significantly in hooks and composability, evolving from a “developer tool” into an “AI Agent runtime.”

Codex CLI focuses on sandbox security and simplicity, taking an “Apple-style” minimalist approach.

Gemini CLI leverages Google’s ecosystem (Vertex AI, Cloud), pursuing an enterprise/cloud-native path.

6.3 Future Evolution Trends

Section titled “6.3 Future Evolution Trends”

  1. Agent Runtime Evolution — The combination of defer/resume/hooks is building an execution framework that can be embedded in enterprise workflows. Future possibilities include webhook callbacks, external approval system integration, and event-driven architecture.

  2. Long-Session Resilience — The autocompact loop fix, memory leak fix, and 50MB+ session support all indicate that users’ real usage pattern is “open a session and use it all day.” The future demands smarter context management: incremental compaction, importance scoring, and selective forgetting.

  3. Windows as a First-Class Citizen — Multiple consecutive releases with extensive Windows fixes and PowerShell tool additions show Claude Code is taking the Windows developer market seriously.

  4. MCP Ecosystem Maturation — Non-blocking connections, improved error handling, and timeout controls signal MCP’s transition from “experimental protocol” to “production-grade infrastructure.”

  5. Terminal UI Engineering — Alt-screen rendering, virtual scrolling, and tmux compatibility. Terminal AI tool UI quality is approaching that of GUI applications.

  6. Defense in Depth — Symlink path resolution, hook if condition hardening, and PowerShell parameter hardening. Every fix closes a potential security vulnerability.

In one sentence: Claude Code 2.1.89 is a release centered on “hardening” and “composability”—not a flashy pile of new features, but making existing capabilities truly reliable, controllable, and composable. This is the critical step from “fun tool” to “trusted infrastructure.”

Share Claude Code Skills with OpenClaw — A Complete Guide

Apr 1, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Let OpenClaw reuse Claude Code’s installed plugins/skills directly — no duplicate installs, auto-synced updates.

Background

Section titled “Background”

Claude Code (Anthropic’s official CLI) installs plugins via the /install command. Each plugin can contain multiple skills following the AgentSkills specification, with SKILL.md as the entry point.

OpenClaw also supports the AgentSkills format — the two skill structures are fully compatible. By creating symlinks, you can let OpenClaw directly reuse all skills installed through Claude Code.

How It Works

Section titled “How It Works”

Claude Code’s Skill Storage Structure

Section titled “Claude Code’s Skill Storage Structure”

Claude Code stores plugins under ~/.claude/plugins/cache/:

installed_plugins.json records each plugin’s installPath (the currently active version). The cache directory may retain historical versions — always refer to the path in installed_plugins.json.

OpenClaw’s Skill Loading Directories

Section titled “OpenClaw’s Skill Loading Directories”

OpenClaw loads skills from these directories (highest to lowest priority):

PriorityPathDescription
1 (highest)<workspace>/skillsCurrent workspace skills
2<workspace>/.agents/skillsWorkspace-level agent skills
3~/.agents/skillsPersonal global skills
4~/.openclaw/skillsManaged/local skills
5Bundled skillsBuilt-in with the install package
6 (lowest)skills.load.extraDirsExtra directories from config

Same-name skills at higher priority override lower ones.

The Sharing Strategy

Section titled “The Sharing Strategy”

Symlink Claude Code’s skill directories into ~/.agents/skills/ (layer 3):

  • ✅ All local OpenClaw agents can use them
  • ✅ Won’t override workspace-level custom skills
  • ✅ Will override bundled skills (reasonable — Claude Code’s are typically newer)
  • ✅ Symlinks don’t copy files — updates in Claude Code take effect automatically

Step-by-Step

Section titled “Step-by-Step”

Step 1: Verify Claude Code Has Plugins Installed

Section titled “Step 1: Verify Claude Code Has Plugins Installed”

Section titled “Step 2: List Skills in Plugins”

Section titled “Step 3: Create Symlinks”

Manual approach (link individual skills):

Automated approach (batch-link all installed plugin skills):

Step 4: Verify

Section titled “Step 4: Verify”

Restart the OpenClaw session or wait for the skills watcher to auto-refresh. New skills will appear in the <available_skills> list.

Auto-Sync Script

Section titled “Auto-Sync Script”

Save the following as sync-claude-skills.py:

Script features:

  • Only processes currently active versions from installed_plugins.json
  • Won’t override non-symlink native OpenClaw skills
  • Automatically cleans up stale symlinks from uninstalled plugins
  • Detects path changes (version hash changes on plugin upgrade) and updates links
  • Idempotent — safe to run repeatedly

Scheduled Auto-Sync

Section titled “Scheduled Auto-Sync”

Option 1: OpenClaw Cron (Recommended)

Section titled “Option 1: OpenClaw Cron (Recommended)”

Create a cron job in OpenClaw to sync every 4 hours:

Option 2: System crontab

Section titled “Option 2: System crontab”

Important Notes

Section titled “Important Notes”

Name Conflicts

Section titled “Name Conflicts”

Different Claude Code plugins may contain same-named skills (e.g., skill-creator appearing in both anthropic-agent-skills and claude-plugins-official). The script uses a first-come-first-served strategy — later discoveries of the same name are skipped.

To specify priority, manually create symlinks to override.

Security

Section titled “Security”
  • Third-party Claude Code plugins should be treated as untrusted code
  • Review SKILL.md contents before enabling
  • Some skills may depend on specific environment variables (e.g., API keys) — configure these in OpenClaw’s skills.entries

Remote Instances

Section titled “Remote Instances”

Symlinks only work locally. To share these skills with remote OpenClaw instances:

  1. Copy skills to the remote machine (rsync or scp)
  2. Or install Claude Code on the remote machine and run the sync script there

Plugin Updates

Section titled “Plugin Updates”

After Claude Code updates a plugin (/install upgrade), the installPath in installed_plugins.json points to the new version directory. Simply re-run the sync script to update symlinks.

Real-World Results

Section titled “Real-World Results”

On a machine with 28 Claude Code plugins installed, the sync script created 135 skill symlinks, covering:

SourceCountExamples
Anthropic Official (document-skills)15+pdf, docx, pptx, xlsx, frontend-design, claude-api
PM Skills40+lean-canvas, SWOT, PRD, OKR, competitor-analysis
Superpowers12TDD, code review, git worktrees, parallel agents
Everything Claude Code25+Django/Spring Boot/Go patterns, security scan
OthersVariousbeads, planning-with-files, episodic-memory

All skills become available in the next OpenClaw session — no additional configuration required.

The Complete Guide to OpenClaw Slash Commands

Apr 1, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Compatible with OpenClaw 2026.3.x+

OpenClaw slash commands are your direct shortcut to the Gateway — no model involved, zero tokens consumed, instant execution. Master them, and you’ve mastered OpenClaw’s control panel.

1. Command System Overview

Section titled “1. Command System Overview”

OpenClaw commands come in three tiers:

TypeBehaviorExamples
CommandsStandalone messages, handled by Gateway/help, /stop, /kill
DirectivesCan be inlined in messages, invisible to model/think, /model, /fast
Text-onlyOnly available in text chat! ls -la, /compact

Key distinction: When sent alone, directives persist to the session; when embedded in a message, they only apply to that single turn. This matters — it comes up repeatedly.

Permission Model

Section titled “Permission Model”

Not everyone can use commands. Authorization chain:

  1. If commands.allowFrom is configured → only this matters, everything else ignored
  2. Otherwise → channel allowlist + pairing + commands.useAccessGroups
  3. Unauthorized sender’s commands → silently dropped, inline /... treated as plain text

Fast Path

Section titled “Fast Path”

Command-only messages (entire message is just the command) take the fast path: no queue, no model, no @mention required (in group chats). This means /stop always works immediately, even while the model is generating.

Section titled “/status — Your Dashboard”

Returns complete session state: model, provider usage/quota, thinking level, elevated status, etc.

Use cases:

  • Check quota: After a heavy task, /status to see remaining Claude credits
  • Confirm config: After switching models, /status to verify
  • Debug slowness: Agent responding slowly? /status to check if thinking got bumped up

Tip: /status is an inline shortcut — write me a script /status returns status first, then processes the message.

/help and /commands

Section titled “/help and /commands”

Forgot a command? Ask anytime. Both support inline usage.

/whoami — Identity Check

Section titled “/whoami — Identity Check”

Alias: /id. Returns your sender id (provider + user identifier).

The Complete Guide to OpenClaw Tools

Apr 1, 2026
Vibe Sparking

A detailed walkthrough of every OpenClaw tool — usage, scenarios, and gotchas.

1. File Operations

Section titled “1. File Operations”

Read — Read Files

Section titled “Read — Read Files”

Read file contents. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp).

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
pathstring✅File path (relative or absolute)
offsetnumber❌Start line (1-based)
limitnumber❌Max lines to read

Note: Text output truncated at 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever first). Images returned as attachments for vision model analysis.

Write — Write Files

Section titled “Write — Write Files”

Create or overwrite files. Auto-creates parent directories.

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
pathstring✅File path
contentstring✅Content to write

⚠️ Completely overwrites the target file. For small changes to large files, use Edit instead.

Edit — Precise File Editing

Section titled “Edit — Precise File Editing”

Exact text replacement in files. Two modes:

Single replacement: oldText + newText

Multiple replacements: edits array with {oldText, newText} objects

Note: oldText must uniquely match; edits must not overlap; modes cannot be mixed.

2. Command Execution

Section titled “2. Command Execution”

Exec — Run Shell Commands

Section titled “Exec — Run Shell Commands”

Execute shell commands with foreground, background, and PTY support.

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
commandstring✅Shell command
workdirstring❌Working directory
yieldMsnumber❌Auto-background after ms (default 10000)
backgroundboolean❌Run in background immediately
timeoutnumber❌Timeout in seconds (default 1800)
ptyboolean❌Pseudo-terminal for TTY commands
hoststring❌sandbox/gateway/node
elevatedboolean❌Request elevated permissions

Use cases:

  • Run scripts: exec("python3 train.py")
  • Long builds: exec("npm run build", yieldMs=1000) — auto-backgrounds
  • Interactive CLIs: exec("htop", pty=true)
  • Remote execution: exec("uptime", host="node", node="my-server")

Process — Manage Background Processes

Section titled “Process — Manage Background Processes”

Manage exec sessions started in the background.

ActionPurpose
listList all background sessions
pollWait for updates (use timeout)
logView process output
writeWrite to stdin
send-keysSend keystrokes (Enter, Ctrl+C, etc.)
killTerminate process

Tip: Avoid rapid poll loops — use poll with timeout parameter.

3. Web & Search

Section titled “3. Web & Search”

Web Search — Internet Search

Section titled “Web Search — Internet Search”

Search the web using DuckDuckGo. Returns titles, URLs, and snippets.

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
querystring✅Search query
countnumber❌Results (1-10)
regionstring❌Region code (e.g., us-en)

Note: No API key needed. Results cached 15 minutes. Returns snippets only — use Web Fetch for full pages.

Web Fetch — Extract Web Content

Section titled “Web Fetch — Extract Web Content”

Fetch and extract readable content from URLs (HTML → Markdown/Text).

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
urlstring✅URL to fetch
extractModestring❌markdown (default) or text
maxCharsnumber❌Max characters to return

⚠️ Does not execute JavaScript — SPAs may return empty shells.

4. Multimedia

Section titled “4. Multimedia”

Image — Image Analysis

Section titled “Image — Image Analysis”

Analyze images with a vision model.

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
imagestring❌Single image path or URL
imagesarray❌Multiple images (up to 20)
promptstring❌Analysis prompt

⚠️ Only use when images were NOT already attached in the user’s message.

5. Sessions & Multi-Agent

Section titled “5. Sessions & Multi-Agent”

Sessions Spawn — Create Sub-Agents

Section titled “Sessions Spawn — Create Sub-Agents”

Spawn isolated sub-agent sessions for background task execution.

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
taskstring✅Task description
modelstring❌Model override
modestring❌run (one-shot) or session (persistent)
runtimestring❌subagent or acp

Note: Non-blocking; sub-agent auto-announces results; max 8 concurrent by default.

Claude Code v2.1.86 Deep Dive: All 28 Changes Explained

Mar 31, 2026
Vibe Sparking

This is a stability and polish-focused release with 28 changes: 1 new feature, 2 optimizations, and 25 fixes/improvements. Here’s the full breakdown.

I. New Features

Section titled “I. New Features”

1. X-Claude-Code-Session-Id HTTP Header

Section titled “1. X-Claude-Code-Session-Id HTTP Header”

Background: Enterprises using API proxies/gateways (LiteLLM, Helicone, Portkey) for cost tracking and rate limiting need to know “which requests belong to the same Claude Code session.” Previously, this required parsing the JSON body’s conversation metadata — fragile and a privacy risk.

Use cases:

  • Enterprise IT aggregates per-developer, per-session token consumption via proxy
  • Security auditing: tracking abnormally high-frequency sessions
  • Example: X-Claude-Code-Session-Id: sess_abc123 → proxy buckets by header directly, no body parsing needed

Notes:

  • Session IDs can be correlated to user behavior; proxy logs need proper anonymization
  • Self-hosted proxies must pass this header through — don’t let WAF rules strip it

Competitive comparison:

ProductSession Tracking
Claude CodeDedicated HTTP header (new)
CursorBuilt-in dashboard, no session-level header
Continue.devNo native solution, requires custom injection
CopilotGitHub backend stats, no proxy-level granularity

Trend: As AI coding agents enter enterprises, observability becomes table stakes. Expect dedicated AI agent APM toolchains (think Datadog for AI agents).

2. .jj / .sl Added to VCS Exclusion List

Section titled “2. .jj / .sl Added to VCS Exclusion List”

Background: Jujutsu (.jj/) and Sapling (.sl/) are next-gen version control systems. Previously, Claude Code’s grep and file completion would dive into these directories, surfacing metadata noise.

Use cases:

  • Teams using Jujutsu for monorepos — @ file completion no longer shows .jj/store/ object files
  • Code search no longer hits .sl/ internal state

Competitive comparison:

  • VS Code: .gitignore-driven, requires manual .jj addition
  • Cursor: No explicit Jujutsu/Sapling exclusion yet
  • JetBrains: Has Jujutsu plugin, but index exclusion needs configuration

Trend: Jujutsu is growing rapidly (already used at scale inside Google). Expect native support across IDEs and AI coding tools by late 2026.

II. Core Bug Fixes

Section titled “II. Core Bug Fixes”

3. --resume Throws “tool_use ids without tool_result blocks”

Section titled “3. --resume Throws “tool_use ids without tool_result blocks””

Background: v2.1.85 changed session serialization format, causing old session restores to have tool_use blocks without matching tool_result — API validation failure. A version compatibility break.

Scenario: Developer creates a long session in v2.1.84, upgrades, uses claude --resume → immediate crash.

Competitive comparison: Cursor and Copilot Chat sessions are short-lived — cross-version resume barely exists. Claude Code’s --resume is a differentiator but carries maintenance burden.

Trend: Agent session resume will become critical. Expect standardized agent conversation serialization formats.

4. Write/Edit/Read Fail on Files Outside Project Root

Section titled “4. Write/Edit/Read Fail on Files Outside Project Root”

Background: When conditional skills or rules are configured, file operations on paths like ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md fail. The conditional skill path validation was too strict, confining all paths to the project root.

Scenario: User maintains global instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md → Agent tries to read/edit → blocked by conditional skill sandbox logic.

Competitive comparison:

  • Cursor: Rules files are project-only — no global rules capability, no issue
  • Windsurf: Similar global + project-level config layering
  • Copilot: Fixed instruction file location, unconditional loading

Trend: AI coding agent permission models will increasingly resemble OS file permissions — allow-lists + layered policies.

5. Every Skill Call Triggers Unnecessary Config Disk Write

Section titled “5. Every Skill Call Triggers Unnecessary Config Disk Write”

Background: Each skill invocation wrote the config file to disk. Especially severe on Windows — NTFS handles frequent small writes poorly, and concurrent writes can corrupt the config.

Scenario: Heavy skill users on Windows find Claude Code getting progressively slower. Worst case: config file corrupted by concurrent writes.

Competitive comparison: Most competitors use in-memory cache + debounced writes. This is an engineering maturity gap for Claude Code.

6. /feedback OOM Crash on Ultra-Long Sessions

Section titled “6. /feedback OOM Crash on Ultra-Long Sessions”

Background: /feedback serializes the entire conversation transcript. Sessions with thousands of turns can produce transcripts of hundreds of MB, causing Node.js heap overflow.

Scenario: Developer works an 8-hour marathon session, tries to submit feedback → process killed.

Competitive comparison:

  • Cursor: Each Composer interaction is independent — no ultra-long sessions
  • Copilot Chat: Implicit session length limits

Trend: Agent “session lifecycle management” will become a product design focus — session pruning, archival, and summarization.

7. --bare Mode Missing MCP Tools + Silently Dropping Messages

Section titled “7. --bare Mode Missing MCP Tools + Silently Dropping Messages”

Background: --bare mode (minimal UI for embedding) had two independent bugs:

  1. MCP tools weren’t injected into the tool list
  2. Messages enqueued mid-turn were silently dropped

Scenario: Embedding Claude Code via --bare in a custom IDE → MCP tools (DB queries, etc.) unavailable. Sending concurrent messages → messages lost without error.

Trend: Claude Code is evolving from “terminal tool” to “embeddable agent runtime.” --bare mode quality directly determines ecosystem ceiling.

III. Terminal UI Fixes

Section titled “III. Terminal UI Fixes”

8-12: Precision Terminal Experience Fixes

Section titled “8-12: Precision Terminal Experience Fixes”
BugRoot CauseImpact
c hotkey only copies ~20 chars of OAuth URLClipboard write length truncationCan’t complete OAuth login
OAuth password input leaks token prefix on narrow terminalsMasked input line-wrap exposes plaintextSecurity issue ⚠️
Plugin script Permission denied (macOS/Linux)v2.1.83 regression, +x not set on filesAll marketplace plugins broken
Statusline shows other instance’s model nameRace condition in shared multi-instance stateUser misjudges current model
Scroll doesn’t follow new messagesScroll lock state not properly resetMust manually scroll to bottom

OAuth token leak (item 9) deserves special attention — a real security vulnerability. In narrow terminals (e.g., split tmux panes), pasting an OAuth code with masked input’s line-wrap logic exposes the first few characters. While insufficient alone for an attack, it’s a risk in shoulder-surfing or screen-recording scenarios.

13-16: Interaction Detail Fixes

Section titled “13-16: Interaction Detail Fixes”
BugDescription
/plugin uninstall n key behaves counterintuitivelyPressing n should mean “don’t keep data” → actually became the uninstall trigger
Blank transcript after pressing EnterRace condition, UI not rendered before response arrives
Ultrathink hint persists after keyword deletionIncomplete state cleanup
Markdown/highlight render cache memory leakLong sessions: cache holds full content strings without releasing

Memory leak (item 16) explains why long-running Claude Code sessions get progressively slower — the markdown renderer’s cache keeps growing.

IV. Performance Optimizations

Section titled “IV. Performance Optimizations”

17. macOS Keychain Cache: 5s → 30s

Section titled “17. macOS Keychain Cache: 5s → 30s”

Background: Each claude.ai MCP connector startup queries macOS Keychain for tokens. With multiple MCPs configured, Keychain calls block the event loop serially, causing startup lag.

Scenario: 5+ MCP connectors configured (GitHub, Jira, Slack, DB, custom) → startup takes several seconds.

Optimization: Cache window expanded from 5s to 30s — multiple connectors share a single keychain query.

18. @ File References No Longer JSON-Escape Raw Content

Section titled “18. @ File References No Longer JSON-Escape Raw Content”

Background: Using @filename to reference files caused content to be JSON string-escaped (\n → \\n, " → \"), needlessly inflating token count.

Scenario: Referencing a 1000-line JSON file → escape overhead adds 10-20% more tokens.

Optimization: Raw strings passed directly — saves tokens, saves money.

19. Read Tool: Compact Line Numbers + Deduplicated Unchanged Reads

Section titled “19. Read Tool: Compact Line Numbers + Deduplicated Unchanged Reads”

Background: Read tool previously returned full content every time, even when unchanged. Line number formatting was also verbose.

Combined impact of items 17-19: For heavy users, these three optimizations can save 5-15% token usage per session — direct cost savings.

20. Improved Prompt Cache Hit Rate for Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry

Section titled “20. Improved Prompt Cache Hit Rate for Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry”

Background: Tool descriptions contained dynamic content (timestamps), causing prompt prefix to differ per request → cache miss.

Optimization: Removing dynamic content makes tool descriptions static → stable prompt prefix → cache hits.

Competitive comparison: This leverages Anthropic’s unique prompt caching. OpenAI’s prefix caching has similar optimization potential, but Cursor et al. don’t expose this level of control.

V. UX Improvements

Section titled “V. UX Improvements”

21-25: Quality of Life

Section titled “21-25: Quality of Life”
ImprovementDescription
Memory filenames now clickable/highlighted”Saved 3 memories” filenames become interactive links
/skills description truncated to 250 charsPrevents long skill descriptions from eating context
/skills sorted alphabeticallyFrom “random order” to “predictable order”
Auto mode shows reason when unavailableFrom vague “temporarily unavailable” to “your plan doesn’t support this”
[VSCode] Long operations no longer falsely report “Not responding”Timeout threshold raised or switched to heartbeat detection
[VSCode] Max plan users downgraded to Sonnet after 8hOAuth token refresh loses plan info

VSCode Sonnet downgrade (item 25) is particularly damaging — Max plan users paying top dollar get silently downgraded to Sonnet after 8 hours, with noticeably lower output quality and zero notification. This severely impacts user trust.

VI. Overall Assessment

Section titled “VI. Overall Assessment”

Release Positioning

Section titled “Release Positioning”

This is a textbook stabilization release with minimal new features, focused on:

  1. Reliability: Resume, OOM, config corruption fixes
  2. Security: OAuth token leak patch
  3. Performance: Token savings, faster startup, memory leak fix
  4. Enterprise readiness: Session ID header, Bedrock/Vertex cache optimization

Competitive Overview

Section titled “Competitive Overview”
DimensionClaude CodeCursorCopilotWindsurf
Terminal-native✅ Core strength❌❌❌
Session resume✅❌❌Partial
Enterprise proxy support✅ New headerDashboardGitHub backend❌
Plugin ecosystem🟡 Growing✅ Mature✅ Mature🟡
Stability🟡 Rapid iteration✅ Relatively stable✅ Stable🟡
VCS breadth✅ Git+Jujutsu+SaplingGit onlyGit onlyGit only

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  1. Agent Runtime Evolution: --bare fixes + Session ID header signal Claude Code evolving from CLI tool to embeddable agent runtime
  2. Enterprise Observability: Session tracking → future spans/traces → full AI agent observability
  3. Session Lifecycle Management: OOM fix is a band-aid; long-term needs session pruning, auto-summarization, segmented resume
  4. Multi-VCS World: Jujutsu support signals the post-Git era — dev tools need to be VCS-agnostic
  5. Token Economics: Three stacked token optimizations show Anthropic is serious about API cost optimization — key to retaining power users
